newsitem.title: UK: WORLD BONDS - T-bond jobs relief may be short-lived.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS - T-bond jobs relief may be short-lived.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries basked in the comfort of last week's soft employment report, but their counterparts in core Europe are likely to jolt them out of complacency soon, analysts said on Monday.

The risk that upcoming U.S. inflation data may be stronger than epxected, coupled with signs that economic recovery in Germany and France is only tottering along, suggests investors may be better off buying Bunds, they said.
"It's going to be difficult for Treasuries to extend the rally further," said Andrew Bevan at Goldman Sachs in London.

"The market has largely taken back any notion at all of a Federal Reserve tightening between now and the first quarter of next year -- so there is no real cushion there," said Bevan, Golman's senior bond economist.
The September jobs report showed 40,000 jobs were lost from the payroll last month versus a downwardly revised 241,000 gain in August. Analysts had expected a rise of 166,000 in September.

But the unemployment rate ticked up only slightly, rising to 5.2 percent in September from 5.1 in August. While T-bonds rallied on the news, with the benchmark 30-year long bond jumping well over a full point, analysts said the reaction was probably overdone.

"What we have witnessed all year is that when Treasuries rally they pull Europe with them, but when the U.S. comes under pressure, Europe has outperformed," said Michael O'Hanlon, chief international economist at PaineWebber in London. "That picture will probably remain for quite some time."
O'Hanlon pointed to a handful of concerns for T-bonds in the coming week, and said a weak jobs report in Germany and growth data in France were likely to shore up debt rallies in Europe.
"There's a risk in the U.S. of a slightly higher retail sales number on Friday than people are anticipating," he said.
The consensus view for retail sales is for a 0.3 percent rise in September versus 0.2 percent in August.
But O'Hanlon said the introduction of new winter lines may have pushed store sales up, and while this posed no inflation threat, he was wary the market might take a firm number badly.

"That coupled with (Minneaopolis Federal Reserve president Gary) Stern -- who will undoubtedly make some cautious hedge comment about a potential inflation push will add to Europe's outperformance of the States this week," O'Hanlon said.
Stern -- the the only dissenting voice when Fed governors voted 11 to one at the August monetary policy meeting to keep U.S. interest rates steady -- speaks in Michigan on Tuesday.

Both Bevan and O'Hanlon said the Bund/T-note yield spread, which has traded around 60 basis points in the past week, should push in Germany's favour in the short term, bloating to around the 75/80 basis point level.
"The technical outlook is very good in Germany for the short-term. But we are taking the view that a 75 basis point US/Bund spread is as far as it goes," said Bevan.
But Mark Capleton, international bond strategist at BZW in London, said outpeformance in Europe was not on the cards.
"Our view is very much that this spread can narrow from here," he said. "Over 12 months we see it closing back to zero, and over the short term that trend should be encouraged."
Capleton said the impetus for the gap slimming would come not so much from bond-positive U.S. news, but from a bond-negative European background.
"With Bund yields now through six percent, there is not a lot of upside left in Germany. Whenever they go through six percent they never stay there for very long," he said.

Capleton also said there was a realisation dawning on the market that a single European currency was likely to be a diluted currency as peripheral European nations fight to get in, if not in the first round, then soon after.
"That dilution should be starting to impact on the German yield curve soon," he said.
-- Kate Kelland, International Bonds Unit +44 171 542 8682
